title: Customer/prospect interview notes — Hosted API onboarding + “production-ready” (Jan 2026)
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- We’re collecting qualitative input to inform (1) the in-product guided onboarding checklist in Console and (2) the “first production launch” definition + docs/quickstarts.
- Primary audience: PM + Design + DevEx + Support.
- Focus: where people get stuck during onboarding, which docs are confusing, what they consider “production-ready” for LLM inference, and what could be validated automatically vs “read + acknowledge”.

Method
- 7 conversations (mix of prospects + new self-serve users + one beta-friendly design partner).
- Notes are summarized (not verbatim transcripts). Where we have an exact quote, it’s marked.
- Most interviews were 25–45 min. Mix of Zoom + async follow-ups.

Participants (anonymized where requested)
1) Aurora Labs (prospect; AI-native startup; platform eng lead + 1 SWE)
2) Northstar Finance (prospect; compliance-heavy; security eng + app eng)
3) PineconeAI (existing customer; early checklist feedback; staff engineer)
4) “SaaS CRM vendor” (new self-serve user; one full-stack eng)
5) “Healthcare analytics” (new self-serve user; ML engineer)
6) “Dev tools company” (evaluating; developer advocate)
7) “Gaming studio” (new self-serve user; backend eng)

Top themes (TL;DR)
1) Fast path is valued, but people still want guardrails: they will copy/paste a quickstart and ship it if the docs imply it’s “safe enough.” They want Redwood to be explicit about what’s demo-only vs production.
2) Authentication + key management confusion is the #1 “wasted hour”: test vs prod keys, project vs org scope, and 401 errors that look like permissions.
3) Rate limits / quotas: 429s surprise users because they don’t know which limit they hit (RPM, TPM, concurrent streams). People want a “what to do next” snippet (retry/backoff + where to see limits) right where the error is.
4) Streaming reliability: disconnects + partial responses create distrust. Customers want a recommended client pattern (timeouts, reconnect behavior, idempotency/request IDs) and clarity on what “success” means for streaming.
5) Docs discoverability: users struggle to find the canonical path; they bounce between API reference, SDK README, and Console. They want one “start here” page with a single golden path per language.
6) Production-ready definition converges on: retries/timeouts, observability, budget controls, safe rollout, and data handling. Less focus on “perfect prompts,” more on operational safety.
7) Trust/privacy: compliance prospects are OK with telemetry if it is explicit, minimal, and never includes prompt content. They want retention controls and a clear statement in the docs + contract.

Detailed notes by interview

Interview 1 — Aurora Labs (prospect)
Date: 2026-01-28 (see Fireflies transcript)
Role/background
- Platform/infra-minded team; they’ve integrated multiple LLM APIs and self-hosted a model before.
- Current pain: inconsistent performance across providers and lack of clarity about rate limiting/throughput.
Onboarding experience / friction
- “Time to first token” matters; they measure success as: first API response + first streaming response in their dev environment.
- They got stuck on auth early: unclear whether API key is scoped to org vs project; they also weren’t sure which region their project was in.
- Quote: “I don’t mind reading docs, but I need one canonical quickstart. When there are three different examples, I don’t know which one is blessed.”
Docs confusion
- They bounced between: Console -> docs -> SDK repo -> back to docs.
- They didn’t know where “recommended defaults” lived (timeouts, retries, max tokens, etc.).
Production-ready definition (their words)
- “Production-ready means I can roll it out gradually and I can tell when it’s failing.”
- Minimum bar they expect a provider to document:
  - Retry/backoff guidance for 429/5xx and timeouts
  - Idempotency strategy or request IDs (so they can trace and dedupe)
  - Latency + error-rate dashboards (even basic)
  - Budget controls / usage caps (or at least alerts)
  - Clear model versioning/pinning guidance
Suggestions for checklist steps
- Make “first streaming response” an explicit step.
- Make “set timeouts + retries” a production step with code snippet.
- Include an explicit “pin a model version” step before prod.
Validation possibilities
- Auto-detect first 200 response for a project.
- Auto-detect a streaming session (SSE/WebSocket) completion.
- If possible: detect “retries enabled” via SDK header/UA? (They didn’t insist; just asked for best practices.)

Interview 2 — Northstar Finance (prospect; compliance-heavy)
Date: 2026-01-18
Role/background
- Security eng owns vendor review; app eng will implement.
- Their primary concern is not speed; it’s governance + audit.
Onboarding friction
- They won’t run “random curl commands” with production-like data. They want a safe sandbox story.
- They asked repeatedly: what does Redwood log by default? (request metadata, tokens, prompts?)
Docs confusion
- Hard to find a definitive statement: “We do not store prompt content” (or if stored, where and for how long).
- They didn’t know if usage analytics implies any content capture.
Production-ready definition
- Minimum bar for them:
  - Explicit data handling statement (no prompt/response content in telemetry)
  - Retention policy and ability to configure retention for operational logs
  - Audit logs for key actions (key creation, permission changes)
  - Environment separation (dev vs prod keys; ability to restrict prod keys)
  - Region/data residency controls
- Quote: “If the provider can’t explain what they collect in one page, we assume worst-case.”
Suggestions for checklist steps
- Add a step: “Review data handling + telemetry” (even if it’s just a doc deep link + checkbox acknowledgement).
- Add a step: “Create a prod API key” with clear permissions and a “do not use in client-side” warning.
Validation possibilities
- They’re okay with non-validated steps for compliance items, as long as they’re explicit and link to the right doc.

Interview 3 — PineconeAI (existing customer; early design partner)
Date: 2026-01-23
Role/background
- Staff engineer; owns integration patterns and reliability.
What worked
- They like Console as the “home” for keys + usage; they just need it to guide them more.
Onboarding friction
- Streaming disconnects bit them early. They weren’t sure if it was their network, their client implementation, or Redwood.
- They want guidance on “what is a normal streaming failure mode and what do I do”.
- Rate limits: they hit 429 during a load test and didn’t know whether it was concurrency or TPM.
Docs confusion
- Error docs are too generic; they want:
  - “If 401: check X, Y, Z”
  - “If 429: check limits page + retry w/ jitter; consider requesting quota”
  - “If stream disconnect: recommended reconnect + partial output handling”
Production-ready definition
- “We don’t call it prod until it has alerts.” (error rate, latency, cost)
- They also care about rollbacks: “If a new prompt or model version goes bad, we need a switch.”
Suggestions for checklist steps
- Put observability earlier than we thought (immediately after first success).
- Add a step: “Set up usage alerts / budget guardrail” (even if minimal in phase 1).
Validation possibilities
- Detect “visited usage dashboard” is useful.
- They suggested adding a “copy tracing/request id” snippet that flows through logs.

Interview 4 — SaaS CRM vendor (new self-serve user)
Date: 2026-01-12
Role/background
- Full-stack engineer; not an ML specialist.
Onboarding friction
- Biggest issue: they accidentally used the wrong key/environment (they had multiple tabs open).
- 401 errors felt like “the API is down” rather than “I am unauthorized.”
- Quote: “If I get a 401, just tell me exactly what to click.”
Docs confusion
- They did not understand the difference between “project” and “org” quickly.
- They didn’t realize keys are per-project (or whichever the actual model is); they requested clearer UI copy and docs.
Production-ready definition
- Simple:
  - Don’t leak keys
  - Handle errors
  - Have a dashboard to see usage
- They were receptive to a short “prod checklist” if it’s not too scary.
Suggestions for checklist steps
- “Create your first API key” should include a warning about client-side use.
- “Test vs prod” distinction is necessary and should be visible in the UI.
Validation possibilities
- “Key created” can be validated.
- Potentially validate “prod key created” when they label it prod.

Interview 5 — Healthcare analytics (new user)
Date: 2026-01-15
Role/background
- ML engineer prototyping in notebooks; will hand off to backend team.
Onboarding friction
- They want copy/pastable notebook examples. They found snippets but not a full workflow.
- They were unsure about default timeouts and how to set them in the SDK.
Docs confusion
- They want the docs to say “here is the minimal safe client skeleton.”
- They asked for explicit examples of structured output and tool calling basics because it reduces app-side parsing bugs.
Production-ready definition
- “Production-ready is when it stops being a notebook.”
- Needs: containerizable sample, environment variables, and a clear error-handling path.
Suggestions for checklist steps
- Keep advanced steps (tool calling, structured output) optional/expandable so it doesn’t block the core funnel.
Validation possibilities
- They didn’t care about validation; they cared about “one blessed sample.”

Interview 6 — Dev tools company (evaluating; dev advocate)
Date: 2026-01-20
Role/background
- Evaluates APIs from the perspective of making tutorials and demos.
Onboarding friction
- They said onboarding is “too many choices.” They want:
  - One quickstart per language
  - One recommended model for first request
  - One canonical snippet for streaming
Docs confusion
- They want consistent terminology:
  - “API key” vs “token”
  - “Project” naming and what it means
- They suggested adding “copy code” buttons everywhere and making sure it compiles.
Production-ready definition
- For their audience: “It works reliably at moderate scale without surprising bills.”
- They emphasized “cost visibility” as part of production.
Suggestions for checklist steps
- Add a step: “Understand pricing / token usage” (link to usage dashboard + pricing doc).
Validation possibilities
- Track “clicked to copy” as an internal metric (not necessarily in checklist).

Interview 7 — Gaming studio (new user)
Date: 2026-01-27
Role/background
- Backend engineer integrating LLM for NPC dialog.
Onboarding friction
- Their first experience was a 429 during a burst test; they interpreted it as instability.
- They asked: “Should I queue requests? batch? what’s the recommended pattern?”
Docs confusion
- They couldn’t find an answer to “how many concurrent streams can I run” without digging.
Production-ready definition
- “Production-ready means it degrades gracefully.”
- They want clear fallback guidance: what happens if model is overloaded; what can they do client-side.
Suggestions for checklist steps
- Include a rate-limit education step with a short explanation + code snippet.
- A “safe rollout” step resonated if described simply (ship behind flag, start with small %).

Cross-cutting pain points (ranked)
1) Auth & keys
- Confusion points:
  - test vs prod key separation
  - which key to use where
  - where to store keys (env vars) and warnings about browsers
  - 401 errors don’t clearly map to actions
- Impact: causes early abandonment or support tickets (observed in Support anecdotes).

2) Rate limits / quotas
- Confusion points:
  - which limit triggered the 429
  - where to see limits in Console
  - how to implement backoff correctly
  - expectation-setting: 429 is normal when exceeding quota
- User request: provide a “known-good” retry snippet in each SDK and a docs page that explains common cases.

3) Streaming
- Confusion points:
  - how to detect completion vs disconnect
  - what to do with partial outputs
  - how to log/trace a streaming request
- User request: stable streaming examples and an explicit troubleshooting section.

4) “Production-ready” is operational, not model quality
- Common minimum checklist items people named (in their language):
  - retries w/ jitter + timeouts
  - monitoring: error rate, latency, cost
  - usage caps or alerts
  - rollout / rollback plan
  - key safety and environment separation
  - data handling statement (especially regulated prospects)

Implications for the Console checklist (Phase 1)
- Checklist should be progressive and not block the “aha moment” (first response), but should keep the path to production explicit.
- Suggested step ordering (rough):
  1) Create API key (show test vs prod concept early)
  2) Make first request (copy/paste snippet)
  3) Try streaming (optional but recommended; many equate streaming with “real app”)
  4) Handle errors (retries/timeouts + link to troubleshooting)
  5) Understand rate limits/quotas (where to see them + 429 guidance)
  6) Visit usage dashboard (cost visibility)
  7) “First production launch” group (rollout, monitoring, key hygiene, model pinning)
  8) Privacy/telemetry (for some cohorts, make visible but not scary)

What can be validated automatically (based on interviews)
- “Key created” (test key)
- “Prod key created” (if we add label/type)
- “First successful request” (per project)
- “First streaming session” (per project)
- “Visited usage dashboard”

What should likely be education / acknowledge steps (not validated)
- “Read data handling / telemetry statement” (esp. for prospects in regulated industries)
- “Set up alerts / monitoring” (until we have deeper integrations)
- “Safe rollout plan” (unless we build explicit rollout features into Hosted API flow)

Open questions raised by users (to resolve in PRD/Docs)
- What is Redwood’s recommended default timeout? (and per SDK how to set it)
- What exactly do we log for request metadata? Do we store prompts/responses anywhere by default?
- For streaming: what guarantees exist? Is there a request ID we can use consistently across logs/support?
- Rate limits: can we show “you hit X limit” in the error response and in Console?
- Model pinning/versioning: how should users do it today, and where is it documented?

Action items (initial)
- DevEx/SDK: ensure retry + timeout snippets are consistent across Python/TS/Go and referenced from checklist steps.
- Docs: create a single “Start here” onboarding landing page per language (or one page that branches cleanly).
- Console: make test vs prod key UI explicit + add inline guidance to reduce 401 support tickets.
- Support: align macros with new troubleshooting docs once published.

Notes to self (George)
- When we write microcopy, don’t say “production-ready” as a vague badge; describe concrete behaviors (“handles rate limits”, “has monitoring”, “can roll back”).
- Make the checklist feel like forward momentum, not a compliance training.
- Consider cohort-specific copy: regulated prospects care more about telemetry/data handling; startups care more about speed + streaming.
